findings.summary: `org.gradle.java.compile-daemon.jvmargs=-Xmx512m` is not a Gradle property and is silently ignored, so the compile daemon has no heap cap. I scanned every jar in the pinned distribution (gradle-9.7.0, lib/*.jar and lib/plugins/*.jar) for the string `compile-daemon`: zero hits; the only `org.gradle.java.compile*` key Gradle knows is `compile-classpath-packaging`. Unknown `org.gradle.*` keys become ordinary project properties with no warning. The cap build.md asks for is `options.forkOptions.memoryMaximumSize` on `JavaCompile`, which the conventions plugin already configures (binjava.java-conventions.gradle.kts:53) and does not set. check-test-budget.sh greps for the key's presence, never for its effect, so it adds 512 MiB to a sum that nothing enforces.
findings.failure_scenario: A developer or CI runner whose Gradle daemon JVM differs from the JDK 25 toolchain (e.g. JAVA_HOME=21, the common setup) makes Gradle fork a compiler daemon. Because `forkOptions.memoryMaximumSize` is unset, no -Xmx is passed and JVM ergonomics give that process ~1/4 of host RAM -- 8 GiB on the 32 GiB WSL2 box build.md describes. Compiling the ingest module then pushes the session past the 6 GiB ceiling and WSL2 kills an unrelated process, which is precisely the outcome build.md exists to prevent, while `check-test-budget.sh` reports 'limits sum to N MiB, within the 6144 MiB ceiling'.

findings.summary: licenseData emits the POM's raw `<name>` prose, but scripts/check-dependency-licenses.sh greps for SPDX identifiers (`GPL-2\.0|GPL-3\.0|AGPL|SSPL|EUPL|CDDL-1\.0|BUSL`). The two vocabularies barely intersect. Evidence from the report this code produced today: JUnit is recorded as `Eclipse Public License v2.0`, not `EPL-2.0`, and opentest4j as `The Apache License, Version 2.0`. The denied spellings in real POMs are `GNU General Public License, version 2`, `GNU Affero General Public License v3.0`, `Server Side Public License, Version 1`, `Business Source License 1.1`, `COMMON DEVELOPMENT AND DISTRIBUTION LICENSE (CDDL) Version 1.0` -- none of which contain any substring in the deny regex. Fixable on either side, but the producer is the half this diff owns; normalising to SPDX ids here is the smaller change.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone adds a dependency whose POM declares `<name>GNU General Public License, version 2</name>`. licenseData writes `"licenses": ["GNU General Public License, version 2"]` into licenses.json, the deny regex finds no match, check-dependency-licenses.sh prints 'no denied dependency licences', and a GPL library ships in an Apache-2.0 project -- the exact late-discovery cost build.md § Licensing rule 2 says the gate exists to prevent.

findings.summary: The comment claims 'the gate must be able to tell unreviewed from clean', but nothing distinguishes them, and the gate does not look at UNKNOWN at all. Three different states collapse to the same token: (a) a POM with no `<licenses>` block, (b) a POM whose licence is inherited from a parent POM -- the code reads only the artifact's own POM text and never resolves `<parent>`, and (c) a POM that failed to resolve, where the catch at line 128 logs a warning and yields emptyList. This is not hypothetical: the report generated by this code right now records `net.bytebuddy:byte-buddy:1.15.11` as UNKNOWN, because byte-buddy-1.15.11.pom carries no `<licenses>` element and declares `<parent>byte-buddy-parent</parent>`, whose POM holds the Apache-2.0 declaration.
findings.failure_scenario: A copyleft dependency published in the extremely common parent-POM style (licence declared once in the aggregator POM, inherited by every module) is resolved onto a runtime classpath. licenseData finds no `<licenses>` block in the artifact POM, writes `["UNKNOWN"]`, check-dependency-licenses.sh greps only for denied names and reports success. The same happens if Maven Central is briefly unreachable for one coordinate: the exception is swallowed into a warning on stdout that no gate reads, and the dependency is recorded as UNKNOWN and passes.

findings.summary: Nothing wires `licenseReport` into any task the build or the hooks actually run: `check` depends on `test` only (verified with an init-script probe of :format:check), and licenses.json lives under `build/`, which .gitignore:2 excludes. Meanwhile making gradlew executable (mode 100755) flips check-dependency-licenses.sh out of its `warn` branch into `fail` on a missing report, and .pre-commit-config.yaml runs that hook with always_run on every commit. So the report is either absent or arbitrarily old, and nothing detects the second case.
findings.failure_scenario: Two concrete failures. (1) Fresh clone or `git clean -xdf`: the first `git commit` aborts with 'no licence report at build/reports/licenses/licenses.json -- run the licence-report task first', and nothing in the repository tells the developer or a CI job that `./gradlew licenseReport` must run first. (2) The stale case, which is worse: an existing tree has a licences.json generated before a new dependency was added. Someone adds an AGPL library to ingest/build.gradle.kts and commits; the hook greps the old report, which does not mention the new dependency at all, and passes. The gate reports on a dependency set that no longer exists.

findings.summary: The guard `if (id.group.isEmpty()) return@forEach   // this project itself` never fires: project dependencies resolve with group `opensearch-bin-ingester` (the rootProject.name), not an empty string. The comment describes behaviour the code does not have. Confirmed by running `./gradlew licenseReport`: the merged report contains nine entries such as `opensearch-bin-ingester:binstore-spi:unspecified` tagged UNKNOWN, and the run emits 20 `licenseData: cannot read POM for opensearch-bin-ingester:...:unspecified` warnings from pointless detached POM resolutions against Maven Central.
findings.failure_scenario: The obvious hardening of B3 -- make check-dependency-licenses.sh fail on UNKNOWN so 'unreviewed' is distinguishable from 'clean' -- is blocked, because the report is guaranteed to contain nine UNKNOWN entries for the project's own modules. Whoever attempts that fix sees the gate fail on binstore-spi and concludes UNKNOWN cannot be made fatal, permanently entrenching the vacuous pass.

findings.summary: Only configurations whose name ends in `RuntimeClasspath` are scanned, so `compileOnly`, `annotationProcessor` and `compileClasspath`-only dependencies are absent from the report entirely -- not UNKNOWN, absent. The `plugin` module will take the OpenSearch 3.8 ingestion SPI as a compileOnly dependency (that is the standard shape for an OpenSearch plugin, and the whole point of architecture.md dependency rule 2 keeping the plugin's surface minimal), and none of it will ever be reviewed. The name-suffix heuristic is also silent when it stops matching: if a future Gradle renames or a plugin adds differently-named resolvable configurations, module.json is written empty, the root task's `filter { it.exists() && it.length() > 0 }` at build.gradle.kts:21 drops it, and the merged report is a well-formed empty array that the gate happily accepts.
findings.failure_scenario: M2 adds `compileOnly("org.opensearch:opensearch:3.8.0")` plus its transitive compile-time closure to plugin/build.gradle.kts. licenses.json never mentions any of it, so check-dependency-licenses.sh reports 'no denied dependency licences' for a module whose compile classpath was never examined, and the build.md distinction between 'we looked and it was fine' and 'we never looked' -- quoted verbatim in the comment at line 99 -- is answered wrongly.

findings.summary: No `distributionSha256Sum` is pinned for the Gradle 9.7.0 distribution. `validateDistributionUrl=true` only checks that the URL looks like a Gradle distribution URL; it verifies nothing about the bytes that come back. The wrapper jar is committed, so the integrity of the downloaded zip is the remaining unverified link in a build that every agent and CI job executes.
findings.failure_scenario: A developer or CI runner behind a transparent proxy, a poisoned mirror, or a compromised services.gradle.org edge downloads a modified gradle-9.7.0-bin.zip. The wrapper extracts and executes it with no integrity check, and every subsequent build -- including the ones that produce the artifacts this project ships -- runs attacker-controlled code, with no diff and no gate showing anything changed.
